'''''Eucalyptus nicholii''''', commonly known as the '''narrow-leaved black peppermint''' or '''willow peppermint''',<ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Approved Conservation Advice for ''Eucalyptus nicholii'' (Narrow-leaved peppermint) |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/20992-conservation-advice.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of the Environment |access-date=2 August 2019}}</ref> is a species of small to medium-sized tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to New South Wales. It has thick, rough, fibrous bark on the trunk and branches, small, narrow adult leaves, flower buds arranged in groups of seven, white flowers and small, hemispherical, bell-shaped or conical fruit. [[File:Eucalyptus nicholii buds.jpg|thumb|225px|Flower buds]][[File:Eucalyptus nicholii fruit.jpg|thumb|225px|Fruit]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus nicholii'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|15-18|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has thick, rough, fibrous, yellowish-brown to grey-brown bark with red-brown underlayers. The bark is coarsely fissured on the trunk and branches, but the outer branches sometimes have smooth bark that is shed in short ribbons. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have dull, greyish, linear to narrow lance-shaped leaves {{cvt|20-64|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-10|mm}} wide. Adult leaves are the same dull greyish green on both sides, narrow lance-shaped, {{cvt|60-140|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-12|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|5-15|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in leaf axils in groups of seven on an unbranched [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long, the individual buds on [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicels]] {{cvt|2-4|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval, {{cvt|3-5|mm}} long and {{cvt|2-3|mm}} wide with a conical [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs from late summer to early autumn and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody hemispherical, bell-shaped or conical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-4|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with the valves protruding slightly above the rim of the fruit.<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus nicholii'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_nicholii.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity |access-date=31 May 2020}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus nicholii'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20nicholii |publisher=Flora of Australia. Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=2 August 2019}}</ref><ref name=sprat>{{cite web|url=http://www.environment.gov.au/cgi-bin/sprat/public/publicspecies.pl?taxon_id=20992|title=''Eucalyptus nicholii'' — Narrow-leaved Peppermint, Narrow-leaved Black Peppermint|access-date=19 October 2016|work=Species Profile and Threats Database|publisher=[[Commonwealth of Australia]]}}</ref><ref name=FGE>Brooker, M.I.H. & Kleinig, D.A. ''Field Guide to Eucalyptus'', Bloomings, Melbourne 2001</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus nicholii'' was first formally described in 1929 by [[Joseph Maiden]] and [[William Blakely]] in Maiden's book, ''A Critical Revision of the genus Eucalyptus''. The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] honours Maiden's private secretary and "Chief Clerk, Botanic Gardens", Richard Nicol.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus nicholii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455047|publisher=APNI|access-date=2 August 2019}}</ref><ref name="Maiden">{{cite book |last1=Maiden |first1=Joseph |title=A Critical Revision of the genus ''Eucalyptus'' (Volume 8) |date=1929 |publisher=New South Wales Government Printer |location=Sydney |pages=52–53 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/123314#page/82/mode/1up |access-date=2 August 2019}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
The narrow-leaved black peppermint grows in shallow, relatively infertile soils overlying shale and slate bedrock usually as part of grassy or sclerophyll woodlands, in association with ''[[Eucalyptus andrewsii]]'' and ''[[Eucalyptus caliginosa]]''.<ref name=sprat/> Its distribution is limited to the [[Northern Tablelands, New South Wales]], particularly in the [[Walcha, New South Wales|Walcha]] to [[Tenterfield, New South Wales|Tenterfield]], area and to the east. The species is sparsely distributed, but most commonly occurs in the central areas of its range.<ref name="FGE" /><ref name="sprat" />

==Conservation status==
This eucalyptus is listed as "vulnerable" under the Australian Government ''[[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]]'' and the New South Wales Government ''[[Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016 (NSW)|Biodiversity Conservation Act 2016]]''. Most specimens occur on private property or on roadsides and few are conserved in nature reserves. The main threats to the species are land clearing and [[habitat fragmentation]], inappropriate fire regimes, grazing by livestock and feral goats, road maintenance and collection of firewood. The entire population is known from fewer than 40 localities, with most not reserved in national parks or state forests.<ref name="environment" /><ref name="OEH">{{cite web |title=Narrow-leaved black peppermint - profile |url=https://www.environment.nsw.gov.au/threatenedspeciesapp/profile.aspx?id=10302 |publisher=New South Wales Government Office of Environment and Heritage |access-date=2 August 2019}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
This tree is very widely planted as an ornamental in southeastern Australia, the fine, dense foliage being particularly attractive.<ref name="FGE" /> It was often recommended as small enough to be suitable for planting on suburban blocks. However, when well-watered it sometimes grows inconveniently tall, and may shed large branches. Hence it sometimes appears on lists of problematic trees for suburban gardens.<ref>See for instance the list of [http://www.cavrep.com.au/P/PROBLEMATICTREES.html Problematic Trees] in the Caverep ''Handbook of Real Estate and Property''.</ref>
